# How to Use Gmail Labels (and Let AI Handle Some of the Sorting)

> **In short:** Gmail labels work like digital tags you stick on emails — one email can have many labels at once. Combined with Gmail's built-in AI categorization (the Primary, Promotions, and Social tabs) and simple filters, you can keep your inbox tidy without touching every message.

If your inbox feels like a junk drawer of receipts, newsletters, and old conversations, Gmail labels are the simplest fix you've never tried. Think of them as digital sticky notes you can slap on any email, group however you like, and find in seconds later. Once set up, much of the work runs itself.

## What Gmail labels actually are (and how they differ from folders)

Most email systems use folders: you drag a message into one folder, and it leaves your inbox. Gmail works differently. A label is more like a tag — once you label an email "Work" or "Receipts" or "From Mom," that email stays in your inbox but also shows up under that label.

The big advantage: an email can have multiple labels at once. That receipt from your work trip? You can label it "Work" AND "Receipts" AND "2026 Tax." Try doing that with folders.

Gmail comes with a few labels built in: **Inbox, Starred, Sent, Drafts, Spam,** and **Trash**. You'll see them in the left sidebar. The ones you create yourself are called custom labels.

## Step 1 — Find your labels panel and see what you already have

Open Gmail on your computer (the desktop version gives you the cleanest view of labels). Look at the left sidebar — you'll see "Inbox," "Starred," "Snoozed," and "Sent." Scroll down a bit. You'll find a section labeled **Labels** with the option **Create new label** at the bottom.

Click **More** at the bottom of the sidebar if you don't see all your labels right away.

💬 Quick check: You should now see the full list of labels, including any you've created before. If you've never made one, you'll only see Gmail's built-in ones in the list.

You'll know it worked when: you can see **Create new label** at the bottom of the labels list.

## Step 2 — Create your first custom label

Click **Create new label** at the bottom of the Labels section in the sidebar. A small window pops up. Type a descriptive name — something like "Receipts" or "Work projects" — and click **Create**.

💬 Example label name: **Family** — useful for messages from relatives, school updates, and photos you'd want to find later.

A few seconds later, the new label shows up in your sidebar under "Labels." It's now ready to use.

You'll know it worked when: the label name appears in your left sidebar and clicking it opens an empty list (since nothing is tagged with it yet).

## Step 3 — Apply a label to one or more emails

Go back to your inbox. Pick an email — or hold down **Shift** or **Ctrl** (or **Cmd** on Mac) to select several at once. Look at the top toolbar: there's an icon that looks like a little tag. Click it.

A list of your labels appears. Tick the one you want, or type a new name to create one on the fly. Hit **Apply**.

💬 Try this: select any email from a family member, hit the label icon, tick **Family**, and apply. That label stays attached, and you'll see it in your sidebar going forward.

You'll know it worked when: clicking the label name in your sidebar shows the email you just tagged.

## Step 4 — Let filters apply labels automatically

This is where labels really start saving you time. A **filter** is just a rule: "When an email matches X, do Y." You can set up a filter that automatically applies a label whenever matching mail arrives.

Open any email, click the three dots in the top-right corner of the message, and choose **Filter messages like this**. A window opens showing the criteria — usually the sender's address or some words from the subject. Adjust as needed, then click **Create filter**.

On the next screen, tick **Apply the label**, pick a label from the dropdown, and click **Create filter**.

💬 Example filter: any email from your favorite newsletter containing the word "weekly" in the subject → apply the label **Newsletters**.

You'll know it worked when: the next matching email arrives already tagged with your chosen label — no manual work needed.

## Step 5 — Use color so labels are easy to spot at a glance

Once you have a few labels, color helps you scan your inbox faster. Hover over a label name in your sidebar, click the three dots that appear next to it, and choose **Label color**. Pick from the color palette.

This small touch makes the label show up in colored text in your inbox list, so you can spot important messages without even opening them.

You'll know it worked when: label names in your sidebar show in their new colors, and matching colored tags appear next to relevant emails in your inbox.

## Step 6 — Turn on Gmail's built-in AI categorization

This is the easiest step of all, because most of the work is already done for you. Gmail uses machine learning (a kind of AI that learns patterns from data — for example, which emails you usually open, reply to, or ignore) to sort incoming mail into tabs at the top of your inbox: **Primary, Promotions,** and **Social**.

If you don't see these tabs at the top of your inbox, click the **Settings** gear icon (top right), choose **See all settings**, open the **Inbox** tab, and set **Inbox type** to **Default**. Make sure **Categories** has the tabs you want ticked.

💬 Quick tweak: if Gmail keeps putting an email from a real person under "Promotions," drag it to the "Primary" tab — Gmail learns from that move and adjusts its sorting going forward.

You'll know it worked when: the colored category tabs appear at the top of your inbox, and your most personal messages land in "Primary" while newsletters and sales pitches collect themselves in their own tabs.

## Common mistakes

- **Treating labels like folders and "losing" archived mail.** When you label an email and then archive it (the box-with-down-arrow icon at the top), the message disappears from your Inbox view but still lives under its labels. Many people think they've lost it. They haven't — it's just no longer in the Inbox view.
- **Creating too many tiny labels.** "Tax 2025," "Tax 2026," "Tax April," "Tax May" — overlap makes searching harder. Start with broad labels (Work, Personal, Receipts, Newsletters) and add narrower ones only when you really need them.
- **Forgetting that labels and filters are separate.** Creating a label doesn't auto-apply it to anything. You need a filter (Step 4) for that. Without the filter, the label exists but stays empty.
- **Hiding the "Labels" section in the sidebar.** If your sidebar is collapsed or "Labels" isn't visible, click **More** at the bottom of the sidebar to expand it.

## What this means for you

- **If you mostly deal with personal email (family, friends, online shopping):** Start with just three labels — "Receipts," "To Read Later," and "Family." Add a filter for "Receipts" that watches for words like "order," "invoice," or "receipt." That's about five minutes of setup and will quietly save you hours of searching later.
- **If you use Gmail for work or school:** Labels beat folders because you can cross-tag. Try "Project A" and "Project B" — emails about both projects can carry both labels. Add a filter that catches anything from your team or classmates, and you'll never lose track of an important thread again.
- **If you want AI to do more of the sorting for you:** Gmail's machine-learned categories (Primary, Promotions, Social, Updates) already work in the background, and Google has been adding Gemini-powered features (Google's AI assistant) inside Workspace Gmail. Check your Gmail settings to see which AI features are available on your account — consumer Gmail and paid Workspace plans offer different options.

## Wrap-up

Gmail labels are one of those features most people ignore for years, then can't live without once they start. The basic setup — creating a few labels, applying them, and adding one or two filters — takes about fifteen minutes. The payoff is an inbox that sorts itself, messages you can find in seconds, and far less time lost to scrolling.

**Your next step:** open Gmail, create one label that matches something you actually search for often (try "Tax" or "Travel"), and set up a single filter to apply it. Once that works, you'll know how the whole system fits together.
